full_judgment:
3. Being aggrieved thereby the assessee took an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals). As none of the parties appeared in the hearing of the appeal, learned Commissioner (Appeals) by his order dated 25-2-01 disposed of the appeal in the absence of the parties with a direction upon the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to apply simple interest. Then, the assessee took further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. By impugned order, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal with certain modifications in respect of the calculation of the annual value of house property and interest. 

 (ii) Whether, in the circumstances and on the facts of the case, the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in treating the income of the company as income from house property and assessable under section 24 of the Ordinance instead of business income and assessable under section 28 of the Ordinance? and 

 5. Two supplementary affidavits on behalf of the assessee were also filed; one dated 10-2-08 and the other dated 14-2-08. In the earlier affidavit, a certificate issued by the Register of Joint Stock Companies, vendor agreement dated 20-2-81 and an agreement of lease dated 20-3-83 were annexed. It is claimed that the property in question was acquired on lease. 

 8. Mr Nur Hussain Chowdhury, learned Senior Advocate, took us through the assessments and relevant provisions of the Ordinance and submitted the objects for which the company was established was to carry on business by way of acquisition of property, development and letting them out for rent, etc., the Appellate Tribunal was wrong in affirming the assessment of the DCT of the income of the house property under section 24 instead of business income under section 28 of the Ordinance. 

 11. Assessee is stated to be a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 and engaged in the business of taking over property by way of lease and after development of the same by filling earth along with erecting and constructing buildings letting them out on rental. 

 13. Sponsoring members of the company comprise one Alauddin Sikder and his children. Property in question was originally owned and possessed by said Alauddin Sikder. As per the vendor agreement dated 20-2-81, the assessee by verified statement claimed that it acquired the property in question against the allotment of shares of the company to him and from the date of issue of shares right, title and interest in the property in question vested in the company. The assessee thereby has given up its case of acquiring the property in question on lease and that as was made in the affidavit dated 10-2-2008. The property in question has been clearly described in the vendor agreement dated 20-2-01 as land, building, securities and liabilities, whatever Alauddin Sikder had were transferred to the family company by said vendor's agreement. 

 14. So, the moot issue that is facing us is, whether the income from such property could be assessed as property income under section 24 or business income under section 28 of the Ordinance. Before we go into the question of the business activity in pursuance of the objects for which the company was established generating the income, let us first consider the decisions cited. 

 16. The Commissioner of Wealth Tax challenged the direction of the Tribunal for valuation of the assessee's property on the basis of bulk valuation. 

 18.  In the circumstances, this Division held, amongst others, "That being so, it is a kind of trade as contemplated in the definition of a business in sub-section (4) of section 2 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. This income from this property can be separately taxed under section 6(111) of the Income Tax Act as an income from house property, but not as an income from the business carried on through such property." 

 19. Upon such view, it was held that the valuation of the property of the assessee, which carried on business, could only be made under section 8(9) on the basis of bulk valuation and not under section 8(3) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1963. Before conclusion, it has however been expressed that a company owning only a housing estate is presumed to carry on a business through such housing estate. 

 20. In A&A Investment Ltd, the question was whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in treating the income from land under section 33(c) of the Ordinance. The business activity for the income year could not be ascertained from the stated facts. The Commissioner (Appeals) found that letting out of the vacant land and realisation of rent there from was part of business of the company. This Division thereon found that the Commissioner (Appeals) rightly held that the income of the assessee was to be assessed under section 28 of the Ordinance, that is business income, and the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was not justified in upholding the assessment of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. 

 21. In H&Z Complex Ltd, exactly the same question which we are facing in this reference was raised by the Commissioner of Taxes as to whether the Appellate Tribunal was justified in directing to assess the income from business under section 28, instead of income from house property under section 24 of the Ordinance. 

 The assessee in the case was only stated to be engaged in acquiring house properties and letting them out on monthly rental basis for the purpose of earning profit upon which they declared dividend and distributed the same among the shareholders. It was further found from the record that the concerned house property was acquired by the company for the purpose of earning income for its share-holders and, as such, it cannot be said that the income should be treated as property income and assessed under section 24 of the Ordinance. 

 "In this connection, it may further be mentioned that the learned Assistant Attorney-General in course of his submission argues that if the company transfers the house property then the return from sale should be treated as business income. If that be so then we fail to understand as to why the rental income there-from should be treated as property income." 

 24. In order to understand the distinction between the property income and business income reference must first be made to sections 24 and 28 of the Ordinance, which are as follows: 

 24. Income from house property— 

 (1) Tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head "Income from house property" in respect of the annual value of any property, whether used for commercial or residential purposes, consisting of any building and lands appurtenant thereto of which he is the owner, other than such portions of the property as he may occupy for the purposes of any business or profession carried on by him, the income from which is assessable to tax under this Ordinance. 

 (2) Where any such property as is referred to in sub-section (1) is owned by two or more persons and their respective shares are definite and ascertainable, such persons shall not constitute and shall not be deemed to be, an association of persons; and for the purpose of computation of the income of an assessee in respect of that property, only such part of such income as is proportionate to the share of the assessee shall be reckoned as his income from that property. 

 25. Close reading of the above sections would make it clear that section 24 deals with tax of any building and lands appurtenant thereto' which is commonly called and known as house property, and tax shall be payable by an assessee under the head, "Income from house property" on the annual value of such property, whether used for commercial or residential purposes if such assessee is the owner of such property. House property is so universally understood in relation to income tax. An assessee under sections 2(7) and 2(47) of the Ordinance includes a company. If the company is owner of such house property and derives income from rents or otherwise there from, then, tax shall be payable by such company under the head, "Income from house property". Besides, a company may have trading or business income in respect of house property depending upon its objects and business activity of the income year in question. Normally, when the company is not the owner of the house property but earned rent by sub-letting the same, such income could only be charged as business income. Liability to pay tax under section 24 of the Ordinance is of the owner of the house property even if the object of the company is purchasing the landed property in order to promote and develop, say, market thereon. 

 26. Question would far more be clearer from the following cases, one old English case and the other of the Supreme Court of India. In Fry vs Salisbury House Estate Ltd 1930 AC 432, the assessee Company which was formed to acquire, manage and deal with a block of buildings, let out the rooms as unfurnished offices to tenants. The company provided a staff to operate the lifts and to act as porters and watch and manage the building. The company also provided certain services such as heating and cleaning for the tenants if required, at an additional charge. For four years the company was assessed under Schedule-A to income tax on the gross value of the building as appearing in the valuation list. The company admitted its liability to be assessed in respect of profits from the services supplied to the tenants under Schedule-D, but the Crown claimed in making the assessment under Schedule-D to include the rents of the offices as part of the receipts of trade, making allowance for tax assessed under Schedule-A. 

 27. It may be mentioned that the scheme of the English Income Tax Law was to provide for taxation of specific properties under schedules appropriate to them and under a general Schedule-D to provide for taxation of income not dealt with specifically. Schedule-A provides for the taxation of income derived from property in land, Schedule-B for incomes derived from occupation of land, Schedule-C for income derived from Government securities and Schedule-E for income from employment in the public service. The House of Lords held that the rents were profits arising from the ownership of land in respect of which the assessment under Schedule-A was exhaustive and that they, therefore, could not be included in the assessment under Schedule-D as trade receipts of the company. The assessee Company, in the cited case, was the owner of the Salisbury House, and the decision of the House of Lords rested on the view that Schedule-A was exhaustive in respect of profits arising from ownership of land. Section 24, which is analogous to. Schedule-A of the English Act, applies to income from property consisting of buildings or lands appurtenant thereto of which the assessee is the owner. 

 28. In East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd vs C1T West Bengal: [1961] 42 ITR 49 SC, the appellant company was incorporated with the objects of buying and developing landed properties and promoting and setting up markets. The company purchased ten Bighas of land in the town of Calcutta and set up a market thereon. The question which arose for determination was whether the income derived from rents of the tenants of shops and stalls was liable to be taxed as business income under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (analogous to section 28 of the Ordinance) or income from property under section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (analogous to section 24 of the Ordinance). The Supreme Court of India held that the income derived by the company from shops and stalls was income received from property and fell under the specific head described in section 9  which is our section 24. It also observed in this connection: 

 "Income tax is undoubtedly levied on the total taxable income of the tax-payer and the tax levied is a single tax on the aggregate tax-able receipts from all the sources; it is not a collection of taxes separately levied on distinct heads of income. But the distinct heads specified in section 6 indicating the sources are mutually exclusive and income derived from different sources falling under specific heads has to be computed for the purpose of taxation in the manner provided by the appropriate section. If the income from a source falls within a specific head set out in section 6, the fact that it may indirectly be covered by another head will not make the income taxable under the latter head. The income derived by the company from shops and stalls is income received from property and falls under the specific head described in section 9. The character of that income is not altered because it is received by a company formed with the object of developing and setting up markets." 

 29. In the following cases, where the company acquired the property by way of lease and then, developed and realised income by letting out the shops, etc. income was treated to be business income or trading income. In the case of Karanpura Development Co Ltd. vs CIT: [1962] 44 ITR 362, the assessee Company was formed with the objects, inter alia, of acquiring and disposing of underground coal mining rights in certain coal fields. The Memorandum of Association of the company enumerated other objects, such as coal raising, but the assessee restricted its activities to acquiring coal mining leases over large areas, developing them as coal fields and then sub-leasing them to collieries and other companies. The leases were acquired for a term of 99 years and the coal fields were sub-let for the balance of the term of the respective leases minus two days. The company never worked the coal fields with a view to raising coal, nor did it acquire or sell coal raised by the sub-lessees. As against a salami of Rs 40 per bigha which the assessee had paid, it realised from the sub-lessees Rs 400 per bigha as salami. In addition, the assessee charged certain royalties at rates higher than those it had agreed to pay under the head leases. The question which arose for determination was, whether the amount received by the assessee as salami for granting sub-lease constituted trading receipts and the profits there from was so assessable. The Supreme Court of India held that the business activity of acquiring leases and granting sub-leases  were in the nature of trading within the objects of the company and not enjoyment of the property as  landowner. It was observed in this connection: 

 "As has been already pointed out in connection with the other two cases where there is a letting out of premises and collection of rents the assessment on property basis may be correct but not so where the letting or subletting is part of a trading operation. The dividing line is difficult to find; but in the case of a company with its professed objects and the manner of its activities and the nature of its dealing with its property, it is possible to say on which side the operations fall and to what head the income is to be assigned. 

 Ownership of property and leasing it out may be done as a part of business. or it may be  done as land owner. Whether it is the one or the other must necessarily depend upon the object with which the act is done. It is not that no company can own property and enjoy it as property, whether by itself or by giving the use of it to another on rent. Where this happens, the appropriate head to apply is 'income from property' (section 9), even though the company may be doing extensive business otherwise. But a company formed with the specific object of acquiring properties not with the view' to leasing them as property but to selling them or turning them to account even by way of leasing them out as an integral part of its business, cannot be said to treat them as land-owner but as trader." 

 30. In the latest case of S B Mercantile Corporation v. CIT, Calcutta: [1972] 83 ITR 700 SC = (1972) 1 SCC 465, the appellant, a private limited company, was incorporated on January 25, 1955. The objects for which the company was established were in accordance with the Memorandum of Association, amongst others, to purchase, take on lease or otherwise acquire and to hold, cultivate, improve, lease, sell, exchange, mortgage or otherwise, dis-pose of land, houses, mines, minerals, mining and other real and personal property and to deal with the same commercially; and to develop the resources of the same property by building, reclaiming, clearing, draining and otherwise improving, framing and planting on any terms or system that might be considered advisable. 

 32. The appellant Company's activity during the period covered by Assessment Years 1956-57, 1957-58 and 1958-59, was that of developing the demised premises and letting out portions of the same as shops, stalls and ground spaces to shopkeepers, stall-holders and daily casual market vendors. The appellant claimed that its income from the leasehold property for the above mentioned three assessment years should be assessed under section 10 of the Act as letting out of that property was its business authorised by the Memorandum of Association. 

 35. Relying upon aforesaid authorities, the Supreme Court of India held that in the case of income from landed property by the owner company, the income would fall under the specific head described in section 9 (property income) and not under section 10 (business income) even though the company had been incorporated with the object of buying and developing landed property and promoting a market thereon. Section 9, as mentioned earlier, did not apply to the present case because the appellant was not the owner of the property in question. As such, there arose no question in the case of the exclusion of section 10 on the ground that section 9 was the specific head. In the instant case, the revenue relied not upon the specific head given in section 9 but upon the residuary head given in section 12 of the Act. 

 37. Lastly, Mr Noor Hossain Chowdhury strenuously argued that use of 'he' in section 24 of the Ordinance was significant. According to him, house property in the section refers to an individual and could only be owned by an individual. A company could not be conceived to have property income. He wanted a judgment upon such submission. We have already found in the above cases that company may also own a house property and earn income as owner from such house property Let us refer to a case that answers exactly the same question. 

 38. The definition of the word "Business", as given in section 2(4) of the Ordinance includes any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adventure or concern in the nature of trade, commerce or manufacture. The definition of business no doubt, includes the activity of taking a property on lease, setting up a market thereon and letting out the shops and stalls in the market. The important question which arises is, whether the acquisition of the property on lease and letting out of the shops and stalls was in the course of investment or whether it was essentially a part of the business and trading operation of the assessee. Paramount consideration which would weigh is, whether the acquisition of the property was by way of investment and whether the property was let out because of the assessee having a title in the same or whether the acquisition and letting out of the property constituted the business and trading activity of the assessee. 

 "If you once get the individual and the company spending exactly on the same basis, then there would be no difference between them at all. But the fact that the limited company comes into existence in a different way is a matter to be considered. An individual comes into existence for many purposes, or perhaps sometimes for none, whereas a limited company comes into existence for the particular purpose of carrying out a transaction by getting possession of concessions and turning them to account, then that is a matter to be considered when you come to decide whether doing that is carrying on a business or not." 

 40. In H&Z Complex Ltd. the question referred is similar to the question referred to this reference. As is already found that in the case, such income was answered to be business income. What was the business activity in the income year in question was missing. In the judgment, we only find the objects of the company. In general activity, it is stated as objects of the company, the company was engaged in acquiring properties and letting them out on monthly rental basis for earning profit. But the pertinent fact of acquisition, whether by purchase or on lease is also missing. From the above authorities, it must be clear that the nature of acquisition would make all the difference. It is also missing whether the company realised rents as owner or lessee of the property. Moreover, the decision was based on the decision of Free School Street Properties Ltd. where the question of bulk valuation of the property arose in connection with payment of wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act, 1963. In such circumstances, such decision does not have binding precedence. 

 41. Now, back to the facts of the case at hand. We find that the assessee acquired the properties in question by way of vendor's agreement dated 20-2-81 against the issue of shares of the value of the properties. In the latest affidavit dated 14-2-08, it has claimed that after such issue of the shares, the right, title and interest in properties vested absolutely in the assessee. Without any ambiguity, it gave up its case of acquisition of the properties on lease. First paragraph of the memorandum of association, clearly describes the object of acquiring the  properties in question. So, whatever income the assessee earned in the income year in question from the properties under consideration it earned as owner and such income therefore was assessable to tax as "Income from house property" under section 24 of the Ordinance.
